Ceriodaphnia dubia exhibits considerable phenotypic plasticity in response to thermal conditions, a trait that has made it a common subject in zooplankton ecotoxicology. When laboratory populations are reared at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], neonates emerge from the brood chamber at a body length of 0.036 centimeters [Lb = 0.036 centimeters]. This modest length at birth reflects the limited provisioning of the subitaneous egg, from which the yolk-dependent embryo derives its nutrients before the trophic switch to filter feeding. As the juvenile crustacean grows through successive instars, an important developmental milestone is reached when the individual attains a body length of 0.063 centimeters [Lp = 0.063 centimeters] at 15 °C, marking the onset of pubertal development at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This transition from the immature organism to a reproductively viable form is a critical checkpoint in the life cycle, after which the growing juvenile can begin gametogenesis onset and eventually produce its first egg clutch.

The ultimate or asymptotic body length achieved by Ceriodaphnia dubia under stable thermal conditions has been documented with considerable precision. In cohorts maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], adults reach a maximum somatic length of 0.09832 centimeters [Li = 0.09832 centimeters], a value that represents the upper boundary of the size-at-age trajectory under those conditions. This ultimate length is characteristic of the sexually mature adult stage, when most resources are directed toward the production of brooded eggs rather than further somatic expansion. The dry weight of these reproductively active adults, measured after desiccation, reaches a plateau at 6.71 × 10⁻⁶ grams , a substantial increase from the initial mass at birth. The contrast between the ultimate length and the length at puberty underscores the protracted growth phase that occurs between the first reproductive activation and the attainment of final adult dimensions, a pattern commonly observed among cladocerans.

Reproductive output and developmental timing in Ceriodaphnia dubia are strongly governed by water temperature, with the most comprehensive data available for individuals reared at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Under these warmer conditions, embryonic development proceeds rapidly, and the age at birth is a mere 2.0 days [ab = 2.0 days] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This short embryonation period is followed by a similarly accelerated juvenile phase; the time since birth at sexual maturation, or puberty, is just 3.6 days [tp = 3.6 days] at 25 °C at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This remarkably brief pre-reproductive interval is characteristic of r-selected freshwater microcrustaceans and allows population densities to increase dramatically within a single growing season. The synchrony between rapid development and high ambient temperature is a key adaptation for exploiting ephemeral or resource-rich habitats.

The lifetime reproductive potential of Ceriodaphnia dubia is substantial, particularly when individuals are reared under optimal thermal regimes. At a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a single ovigerous female can produce a total of 75.9 offspring  over the course of her reproductive lifespan. Each clutch, released at regular intervals from the brood chamber, contributes to this cumulative fecundity. Concomitantly, the species exhibits a maximum lifespan, or longevity, of 59.0 days [am = 59.0 days] when maintained at 25 °C at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This combination of high fecundity and a compressed lifespan positions C. dubia as a classic ephemeral strategist, capable of rapid population turnover. The natural mortality that eventually terminates reproductive activity appears to be driven by senescence rather than by a sudden breakdown of physiological homeostasis, as post-reproductive individuals often survive for several additional days without producing further clutches.

At the moment of birth, the dry weight of a neonatal Ceriodaphnia dubia is a mere 8.8 × 10⁻⁷ grams , a value that underscores the minimal maternal investment per offspring in this cladoceran. This reduced birth mass is typical of small-bodied branchiopods that produce numerous subitaneous eggs throughout a breeding season. The dry weight at birth stands in stark contrast to the ultimate dry weight of the adult, reflecting over a sevenfold increase in somatic mass during the juvenile and early adult growth phases. Interestingly, the length at birth of 0.036 centimeters [Lb = 0.036 centimeters] recorded at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is comparable to values reported for other congeners when standardized for temperature, suggesting a conserved relationship between egg size and neonate dimensions within the genus. The rapid accumulation of body mass from this minimal starting point is sustained by continuous filter feeding on suspended algae and bacteria, which fuels the high metabolic demands of the growing juvenile crustacean.
